title: Chukat: striking the rock (Numbers 20:7–12)
hookLine: told to speak to the rock, Moses strikes it, and will not enter the land

lines: NO FIGS, NO VINES, NO WATER.
cards: The water is gone, and the complaining starts almost at once. Why did you bring us out of Egypt, the people say, to this terrible place, with no figs, no vines, no pomegranates, and no water to drink?
Moses has heard this speech before. Long before, at a place called Horeb, the people were thirsty, and God told him to strike a rock with his staff, and water poured out. Now he's older.
His sister has just died. And this time, the instruction is different by one word.

teach.b: God tells Moses to take the staff, gather the people, and, in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "speak ye unto the rock before their eyes," so it will give its water. Speak, not strike.

teach.h: HEAR NOW, YE REBELS, AND HE STRIKES.
teach.b: Moses and Aaron gather the people before the rock, and Moses says, "Hear now, ye rebels." Then he lifts his hand and strikes the rock with his staff, twice. Water gushes out, plenty for everyone and their animals.
Then the verdict, in paraphrase: because you did not trust Me, to make Me holy in the eyes of the people, you will not bring this community into the land.

teach.h: RASHI, MAIMONIDES: WHAT WAS THE SIN?
teach.b: What exactly was the sin? The commentators argue about it, and they don't agree. Rashi says it's in the plain story: he was told to speak, and he struck.
Maimonides says it was the anger in hear now, ye rebels, because a leader's anger teaches the people that God is angry.
Others point to the words that came next, which in paraphrase ask: shall we bring water out of this rock? As if the miracle were theirs. Some teachers today add a quieter reading.

teach.h: A NEW GENERATION, A NEW WAY.
teach.b: But a new generation needed a new way of being led, and the old move, the one that had worked before, was no longer the right one.
Whatever the reading, the Torah holds even Moses to the difference between speaking and striking.

how: The waters of Meribah are read in the portion of Chukat, and Jewish commentaries, from Rashi and Maimonides to modern teachers, are studied side by side because they disagree about what Moses did wrong.

o: the complaint about figs, vines and water
statute: the portion where Moses strikes the rock
the rock at Horeb that gave water when struck

games.q: who says what the sin was — tap the pairs.
p: his anger: hear now, ye rebels
shall we bring water, as if theirs

s: God told Moses to strike the rock at Meribah
he was told to speak to the rock before the people's eyes. at Horeb, long before, he was told to strike.
the water still came when Moses struck the rock
it gushed out, plenty for everyone and their animals. the consequence came afterward.
the commentators agree on what Moses' sin was
Rashi, Maimonides and others each point to something different.

games.q: you're Moses. you've been told to speak to the rock. the crowd is angry and thirsty, and you're grieving your sister. what do you do?
o: speak to the rock, quietly, as told.
strike it, the way it worked before.
games.why: he called them rebels and struck the rock twice. the water came, but he was told he would not bring the people into the land.

practice: Think of one place you usually reach for the staff: a raised voice, a sharp word, a slammed door, a cold silence, something that worked once and became a habit.
Picture that moment coming tomorrow, and yourself speaking instead, slowly, in a lower voice. Find the first sentence you'd actually say, and keep it.

wordCard.voice: Chukat. The portion where Moses, told to speak to the rock, strikes it instead, and learns he won't enter the land.
